slides.teacher_cue: New sound — ng. Back of tongue rises to the soft palate — same position as /k/ and /g/ — but air flows through the nose. Voice on. A nasal sound at the back of the mouth — nng. Important rule: ng appears at the END of syllables only — never at the start of a word. Korean has a similar sound ㅇ at syllable endings so production is accessible. The main challenge is the spelling: /ŋ/ is written ng — two letters, one sound.
slides.expected_response: Students produce /ŋ/ cleanly and understand that ng only appears at the end of syllables.
slides.correction_move: Model /n/ — front nasal. Model /ŋ/ — back nasal. Students alternate, feeling the tongue position shift from front to back. Then apply to words.
slides.observation_note: Watch for students adding a /g/ after /ŋ/ — producing 'sing-g'. The /g/ is silent in most accents.

slides.observation_note: Listen for whether students can carry the focus from isolation into a real word.
